feedback: Written before this candidate races. The evidence is iterations 0, 1 and 2. Iteration 1 is the best raced design (324.07): the widened row (x = -0.024 to +0.024 m at y = 0.04 m) lifted oval progress from 0.18 to 0.95 and s-bend progress from 0.14 to 0.38, so keep that row. Iteration 2 changed sensor_size to 0.016 m and also changed base_speed (1.2 to 1.1) and kd (0.6 to 0.8). That confounds the result, so the oval collapse (finish rate 0.70 to 0.00) cannot be attributed to the footprint alone. Slalom line_loss_events fell from 2.0 to 1.75, so the larger footprint did help that track, but not enough to justify the oval loss. I am therefore keeping sensor_size at 0.012 m, as you proposed. The wheel_track 0.10 m test is a reasonable next step, because turn rate is the wheel speed difference divided by wheel_track, so a shorter track gives more yaw per unit of control. I have scaled kp to match, so the race tests the geometry change on a comparable loop gain. Depending on the next race: if oval finishes hold near 0.7 and steering_oscillation stays at or below about 0.3, keep wheel_track 0.10 m. If oscillation rises above about 0.3 with finishes falling, the yaw gain is too high, so try mass 0.6 kg rather than further sensor changes. Body_width does not move the off-track limit within its range, so do not spend a run on it.
requested_changes: Keep sensor_size 0.012 m and the widened row (x = -0.024 to +0.024 m at y = 0.04 m), which gave the best raced score (iteration 1).
Keep the wheel_track 0.10 m test, but read it against the matched kp of 4.5. If the oval keeps its finish rate near 0.7 and s-bend or slalom max_error falls below 0.06 m, keep the shorter track.
If steering_oscillation rises above about 0.3 with finishes falling, try mass 0.6 kg to reduce yaw inertia, and do not move the sensors again before testing it.
